summary.text: Choose a prime divisor and split the odd composite modulus as a maximal prime power \(p^k\) times a coprime factor: if the latter is \(1\), then \(k\ge2\), and applying the \(\pm1\) condition to the unit \(1+p\) modulo \(p^k\), then reducing modulo \(p^2\) and using \((1+p)^n=1+np\), forces either \(p\mid n\) (contradicting \(p\mid 2n+1\)) or \(p=2\) (contradicting oddness). Otherwise, from a putative base with power \(-1\), the Chinese remainder theorem constructs a unit whose power has components \((-1,1)\), which is neither global sign because both odd coprime factors exceed \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
m=2n+1.
\]
The sequence value in question is
\[
a(n)=\#\bigl\{b\in\{1,2,\ldots,m-1\}:b^n\equiv-1\pmod m\bigr\}.
\]
Assume that \(m\) is an absolute Euler pseudoprime in the sense of the statement. Thus

1. \(m>1\);
2. \(m\) is not prime; and
3. for every integer \(c\) coprime to \(m\),
   \[
   c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv 1\pmod m
   \quad\text{or}\quad
   c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod m.
   \]

Since \(m=2n+1\), we have
\[
\frac{m-1}{2}=n.
\]
Consequently every unit \(x\) in \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) satisfies
\[
x^n=1\quad\text{or}\quad x^n=-1. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, choose the standard integer representative of \(x\). It is coprime to \(m\) precisely because \(x\) is a unit, so the defining property applies. Also, \(m>1\) and \(m=2n+1\) imply \(n>0\). Finally, \(m\) is odd.

We will show that no residue \(b\) can satisfy \(b^n=-1\). In fact, after factoring the composite number \(m\), either of the two possible forms of its factorization contradicts (1).

We first record the elementary square-zero calculation used in the prime-power case. In any commutative ring, if \(z^2=0\), then for every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
(1+z)^r=1+rz. \tag{2}
\]
This follows by induction. It is clear for \(r=0\). If it holds for \(r\), then
\[
(1+z)^{r+1}=(1+rz)(1+z)
=1+(r+1)z+rz^2
=1+(r+1)z.
\]

Now choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), which exists because \(m>1\). Let \(k\geq1\) be the exact exponent of \(p\) in \(m\), and put
\[
v=\frac{m}{p^k}.
\]
Then
\[
m=p^k v,\qquad \gcd(p^k,v)=1. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, exactness of \(k\) means that \(p^k\mid m\) but \(p^{k+1}\nmid m\). The first divisibility gives the displayed factorization. If \(p\mid v\), then \(p^{k+1}\mid p^kv=m\), contrary to the maximality of \(k\). Thus \(p\nmid v\), and since the only prime divisor of \(p^k\) is \(p\), this proves the coprimality in (3).

Because \(v\) is positive, there are two cases.

## Case 1: \(v=1\)

Here
\[
m=p^k.
\]
We must have \(k\geq2\). Indeed, if \(k=1\), then \(m=p\) would be prime, contrary to the hypothesis that \(m\) is not prime.

Consider the residue
\[
x=1+p\pmod{p^k}.
\]
It is a unit modulo \(p^k\). To see this, any common divisor of \(1+p\) and \(p\) divides their difference \((1+p)-p=1\); hence \(\gcd(1+p,p)=1\), and therefore \(\gcd(1+p,p^k)=1\).

Property (1), now regarded modulo \(p^k=m\), says that either
\[
(1+p)^n\equiv1\pmod{p^k} \tag{4}
\]
or
\[
(1+p)^n\equiv-1\pmod{p^k}. \tag{5}
\]
Reduce either congruence modulo \(p^2\), which is legitimate because \(k\geq2\). In \(\mathbb Z/p^2\mathbb Z\), the residue of \(p\) has square zero. Formula (2) therefore gives
\[
(1+p)^n\equiv1+np\pmod{p^2}. \tag{6}
\]

Suppose first that (4) holds. Combining (4) and (6) yields
\[
np\equiv0\pmod{p^2}.
\]
Thus \(p^2\mid np\), and cancellation of the positive factor \(p\) gives \(p\mid n\). But \(p\mid p^k=m\), and also \(p\mid2n\). Since
\[
m-2n=(2n+1)-2n=1,
\]
it follows that \(p\mid1\), impossible for a prime.

Suppose instead that (5) holds. Combining it with (6) gives
\[
1+np\equiv-1\pmod{p^2},
\]
so
\[
2+np\equiv0\pmod{p^2}.
\]
In particular \(p\mid2+np\). Since \(p\mid np\), this implies \(p\mid2\). As \(p\) is prime, \(p=2\). But then \(m=p^k=2^k\) is even, whereas \(m=2n+1\) is odd. This too is impossible.

Thus the prime-power case cannot occur under property (1).

## Case 2: \(v>1\)

Set
\[
u=p^k.
\]
Since \(p\geq2\) and \(k\geq1\), we have \(u>1\). By (3),
\[
m=uv,\qquad \gcd(u,v)=1,
\]
with both \(u>1\) and \(v>1\).

We now use a hypothetical residue counted by \(a(n)\). Suppose that some residue \(b\pmod m\) satisfies
\[
b^n=-1. \tag{7}
\]
Because \(n>0\), this already implies that \(b\) is a unit. Explicitly,
\[
b\bigl(-b^{n-1}\bigr)=-b^n=1,
\]
so \(-b^{n-1}\) is an inverse of \(b\).

The Chinese remainder theorem gives a ring isomorphism
\[
\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\cong
\mathbb Z/u\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z/v\mathbb Z.
\]
Write the image of \(b\) as
\[
(y_1,y_2).
\]
Equation (7), read in the first coordinate, gives
\[
y_1^n=-1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/u\mathbb Z. \tag{8}
\]
Moreover, because \(b\) is a unit, both \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are units in their respective rings; in particular \(y_1\) is a unit modulo \(u\).

By the Chinese remainder theorem, there is a unique residue \(x\pmod m\) whose coordinates are
\[
(y_1,1). \tag{9}
\]
This \(x\) is a unit, since each of its two coordinates is a unit. Apply property (1) to \(x\). There are again two alternatives.

If \(x^n=1\pmod m\), then taking the first CRT coordinate and using (9) gives
\[
y_1^n=1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/u\mathbb Z.
\]
Together with (8), this says \(1=-1\) modulo \(u\), or equivalently
\[
2\equiv0\pmod u.
\]
Thus \(u\mid2\). On the other hand, \(m=uv\) is odd, so each factor \(u\) and \(v\) is odd. The only positive odd divisor of \(2\) is \(1\), forcing \(u=1\), contrary to \(u>1\).

If \(x^n=-1\pmod m\), then taking the second CRT coordinate and using (9) gives
\[
1^n=-1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/v\mathbb Z.
\]
Hence again \(1=-1\), now modulo \(v\), so \(v\mid2\). Since \(v\) is an odd positive divisor of \(2\), this forces \(v=1\), contrary to \(v>1\).

Thus in the coprime-factor case there cannot exist any residue \(b\) satisfying (7).

We can now conclude. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(a(n)\neq0\). Since \(a(n)\) is the cardinality of the finite set
\[
\bigl\{b\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}:b^n\equiv-1\pmod m\bigr\},
\]
that set would contain some integer \(b\). Its residue modulo \(m\) would satisfy (7).

Choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) and decompose \(m=p^kv\) as above. If \(v=1\), the prime-power argument shows that the absolute Euler property itself is impossible. If \(v>1\), the CRT argument, applied to this \(b\), gives a contradiction. These exhaust all possibilities because \(v\) is positive.

Therefore the defining set is empty, and hence
\[
\boxed{a(n)=0}.
\]
